query: I'm looking for a compact tire pump that can easily fit in my motorcycle tank bag and work well with tight spaces around the valve stem. I noticed the gauge may not be very accurate, but I want to ensure it can still inflate my motorcycle tires effectively without the hassle of using a larger compressor. Also, how does the locking mechanism work? I want to avoid any confusion when using it during my trips.
ori_review:
You will think you are missing parts, I ordered a 2nd one thinking I was. You're not, just configure the head to how the cardboard sleeve shows. If you're using it on tires you will need to switch the inside part around.
On the lip (locking mechanism on head) UP is Locked, DOWN is Unlocked. So flip the lip DOWN, put the head over your valve stem, flip lip UP once it's on to lock it in place. Yes this is prob opposite of every tire infiltrator you have ever used. This product happens to be reversed. When you are done airing your tire, flip the lip DOWN and wiggle it off the valve stem.
It doesn't feel like it's going to go on at first, just flip the lip Down and wiggle it on, the rubber will stretch around your valve stem I promise.

Yes the gauge is inaccurate, I'm still giving this pump 5 stars for the simple reason that 10 pumps will inflate my motorcycle tire 3-4 pounds! That's pretty incredible.
A lot of folks are criticizing the gauge is hard to read/inaccurate. But I always over fill my tire and use this gauge [[ASIN:B0022ZR3O2 Accugage Dial Tire Gauge with Hose RRA60X]] to let air out to desired level.
Compare your pen drive gauge you got from the gas station to the one above and you will see a 3-4 pound difference, if not more. That's not a big deal in a car or bicycle, but not acceptable on a motorcycle in my opinion (unless in a pinch).

I took this pump on a 1300mi motorcycle trip to the Ozarks. It fit in my tank bag, but I used the included zip-ties and mounted it to the undertail of my sports bike. I'm leaving it on as it's easier to use this then to get out my B&D portable air compressor. No rolling up cords with this pump when I'm done. Also I know this works with my rims. There isn't a lot of space between my valve stem and rim on my Honda CBR and I have issues with some gas station pumps not fitting. Which is frustrating when it's the only thing available. Now I'm a little more self efficient.

ori_review:

The app has a ton, ton of tweaks and settings the user can play with to change how it works, a lot of them oriented towards battery life versus data capture. She had no problem figuring out the settings, getting texts to show on the watch, and changing the face graphics to her liking.
I am still getting life out of my 3 or 4 year old fitbit inspire HR, but if/when it dies I'll go with this or whatever its latest version is at the time. Fitbit has gotten too greedy moving premium features to subscription, I really like this band as you buy once, and nothing is paywalled.

query: I'm looking for a quality Baitrunner that offers good performance without breaking the bank. I've had experience with Shimano Baitrunners and recently tried the Okuma Avenger, but I wasn't satisfied with its quality. I've heard positive things about the Ecooda Maelstrom, especially regarding its smooth operation and drag system. Can you confirm if it's a good option for inshore saltwater fishing and if it holds up well over time? Also, how does the size of the Maelstrom compare to other models, particularly for use with a custom rod? I'm considering the 2000 size to match my setup better.
ori_review:
I'm a huge Baitrunner fan, I've been using the Shimano Baitrunners since the B Models. I've recently moved to the Southwest Florida and have taken to the Inshore Saltwater fishing. I purchased a Shimano OC4000 but then bought a custom built rod 6'10' MH Inshore built (Sewell) and the 4000oc was too big for it. As Shimano don't do a smaller saltwater Baitrunner I hunted around a got an Okuma Avenger ABF B3000 as I read good things about them but the quality wasn't there and I wanted a better reel.

After reading a ton more reviews on the competition I came across the Maelstrom, I decided to take the gamble and ordered the 3000. The quality is really impressive and for the price it blows away the competition. It's smooth, comes with an extra spool and has a high quality drag and casts really well. I've landed Snook and Redfish at around the 2ft size with ease and countless snapper with it.

The things that irritate me about it:

1) When the Baitrunner is set to freeline the click is almost silent.

2) The Baitrunner lever maybe the cheapest part of the reel so we'll see how it stands up to being used at least a couple of trips of times a week.

3) The 3000 size is almost as close to size of the Shimano 4000OC and dwarfs the Okuma ABF 3000 B. I've actually ordered 2000 today (9/1/15) as the 3000 is mismatched on the rod I'm using.

I'm currently using 3000 Maelstrom on a Tackle No8 Hellbent Inshore 7'6' MH or a Star Seagis 7 ft MH. Once the 2000 comes in I will use that on the Sewell rod. I'm now looking at the Maelstrom 5000 size to pair with an Extra Heavy inshore as I'm not sure I'll buy another Shimano Baitrunner again.

If you're looking for a low cost good quality Baitrunner I would recommend the Ecooda Maelstrom without hesitation.

How easy is it to set up by myself, and are there any tips to ensure it stays secure and doesn't damage the fabric while packing it away? Also, does it provide good ventilation and shade during hot days? Any experiences or recommendations would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Super easy to set up once you have done it a few times. Some reviews here have said that it's difficult without two people but if you follow the instructions which say to stake down the back two corners and then the front two corners you're solid. Do not attempt to put back pole up inside of the tent - it will tear through the tent fabric -- Instructions/pictures are not clear about having the back pole on the exterior of the back mesh wall. Another thing to ensure that it taught enough ...is ensuring the measurement and placement of front corners.

Super easy to set up. I have only used it in my backyard a few times but it held up perfectly through a few light rain showers and some solid wind gusts. It worked well in keeping sun out -- living in South Carolina we get some hot days even in February -- it worked will in that regard especially with the mesh bottom portions of the side walls that also have the vents on both sides, and the entire side triangular back wall is mesh allowing a maximized flow of air.

There is one tiny con, but it's more of a user error. It's important to fold it back small and tight and ensure you don't snag the bag zipper on the tent fabric because it will catch on the fabric if not super delicate when packing back up -- so don't speed through packing up. I will say a good strategy to avoid this is packing the tent/tarp first then placing the stake/guy line/pole bags on top of the tent so when you zip if it catches on any fabric it will be the fabric of the light weight bag enclosed to hold the poles.

I would highly recommend for any type of light daily use in parks, sporting events, tailgating (although you must have enough space since it is rather large), car camping, or even in the backyard for the kids to have a little shade while running around the neighborhood during a sunny day.

query: I'm looking for a waste treatment product that can effectively manage odors during camping trips. ori_review: We did a 5-day self-supported touring kayak trip in Lake Powell with 10 people and used this as part of our toilet system in conjunction with a Playberg folding toilet seat and Cleanwaste wag bags. I used a plastic bag from the wag bag system over the seat and tied a corner--just like setting up a garbage bag in a garbage can.  The wag bags come with a similar desiccant pre-packaged in the bottom, but I set up a lid on the toilet so the group could use the same bag more than once. I had people add powder as they went. I changed the bag out about every night.  It does not have any type of deodorizing scent, with the lid on the toilet and being away from camp odor remained low--not sure how it would do in really close quarters unless you had a pretty tight fitting lid.  I then transferred the used wag bags into tight Ziploc bags (that come with the wag bags) and into a sealed canister that I had. I had asked people to try not to urinate into the bag to avoid too much liquid.  When I transferred the bags back out later I did not get any liquid or leakage of any kind. The powder did it's job. other people have mentioned similar products you can find at RV supply stores I'm not sure if there is a cheaper more generic bulk product that might be less expensive if you use this regularly, but for my trip this package was more than enough I could have probably used half given the wag bags already started with some in them. query: I'm looking for a high-quality survival knife with a serrated edge, and I've heard great things about the Gerber Prodigy Tanto. How is the overall build quality and grip compared to other Gerber knives? I'm also curious about the sharpness out of the box and whether the sheath is secure enough to prevent accidental slips. Additionally, any insights on whether the handle material feels sturdy would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Bought from Amazon, shipped/sold by Amazon.

Just recently i got bit by the blade bug (it was quite painful), and I've been building a small collection of what i would like to call my "survival/home defense kit".

Gerber has been around for some time now and even though they have factories in China (still awesome Gerber knives made in China), Their high-end made knives are manufactured in Oregon. They've been making knives for the US Army since the 1960's..

I have a few Gerber pocket knives all in which are made in China, but that doesn't necessarily make them bad, they are actually all damn good with very sharp blades..

This one, called the Prodigy is made superbly, it feels wicked in the hand, the steel and just overall build quality and feel is pretty damn great! The tanto point with serrated edge is really nice and really makes it look sexy!
The blade is sharp, but not ultra sharp. it definitely needs to get professionally re-edged!
The edge of the blade out of the box was perfect, not chipped or rounded, straight lines all the way through!

It's full tang all the way down to the butt of the handle and even that looks like it would mess somebody's day up real bad.

The grip/handle is good but not great! I have the Strong Arm Gerber knife and the grip on that beast beats this one leaps and bounds!
The Tac-Hide material feels a bit thin, not crappy thin, just thin. It's strong to a point, just don't abuse it.
The butt end of this knife where the grip material ends seems like its peeling, it's just a hair bit, but i wont mess with it and it should stay on.
The plastic mold is solid, it does look like a 2 piece mold though.

The sheath is super ultra tight with knife inserted, hopefully it weakens overtime. Great to know it wont fall out by accident or force!
Sheath is bi-directional, so you can insert it point in with blade left or right.

It's really just so affordable, not cheap!

Update**, i bought another one! So i now have 2 Prodigy Tanto's!

Picture i uploaded is of the Gerber Prodigy Tanto, Gerber Strong Arm Spear Point, and Bear Grylls Compact Fixed Blade.

query: I'm looking for a brake set that allows for manual toe-in adjustment and performs well at high speeds, especially during descents. Can you recommend a reliable option that offers good quality for the price and has a long lifespan?
ori_review: I upgraded this year to Ultegra on my road bike. I bought these to replace functional but soft no-name brakes. The install I did myself and it was fine. All the parts you need even the wire end nibs are included. You need to be sure you have STI shifters and levers (shift and brakes together). The install took about 30 minutes and then 20 min of riding and fine tuning. The very cool aspect of these brakes is that you can manually set the toe in. If you descend at any kind of speed, this is critical. You don't want fishtail at 40+ mph. Toe-in allows you to ease the brakes on and have the soft touch required for high speed turns and descents. query: I'm looking for an electric scooter that is easy to charge and has a good braking system. I want to make sure it can handle slight bumps and has a decent speed, ideally around 15 mph. Also, how easy is it to fold and carry? I want something durable with a good battery life that I can use for commuting. Any tips on adjusting the brakes or maintaining the scooter would be appreciated!
ori_review:
I started rising bird scooters about a year ago and always thought about how convient they are. Fast forward and I no longer have a company car but a train near home that takes me close enough for a 50 minute walk to work. Tried it and didn’t like it. Looked into getting a scooter or bike. Ordered a kick scooter and after 30 min uphill returned it the same day.

Moving into electric scooters, i researched them for a good two weeks. Segway, exooter and all the popular ones and not so popular ones. Then after ten YouTube videos i saw this one and thought I’d give it a try. A $500 scooter for $300 was not a bad deal. I’ve used it 2 times so far and have this to say:

Charging: very simple plug and wait. Led turns red then green when charged. You can order more chargers from the manufacturer for $20. Take a couple hours but it’s a big battery

Brakes: the electromagnetic brake requires 30 seconds of riding before it kicks in fully. A disclaimer if it doesn’t work instantly. Back brake required some adjustment. It’s a very easy system to under stand. One side of the pad stays put and the other squeezes down. To adjust just unscrew the two top bolts slightly, elevate scooter, spin back wheel and move the brake pad around until it spins freely. Easy i tell you! Don’t return if the back wheel makes noise or doesn’t spin, check the brake first.

Wheels: air filled wheels make it easy to go over slight bumps but going between side walks i caution slowing down when crossing the street or you’ll be slamming the front and will break it. The manufacturer also has replacement and honey comb hybrid wheels that flex but don’t require air. Very smooth ride

Speed: fully charged got up to 18mph. Weigh 180lbs. Speed 1 got me to 13 mph. When you have used 1/4 of the battery the speed goes to 15 mph.

Headlight: bright enough to be seen, not a search beam so don’t know why people complain, it’s a scooter not a patrol car

Folding: easy enough, the commercials and ads won’t include the fact that there’s a safety bolt that needs to be screwed in when unfolded so it doesn’t collapse. You don’t just unfold and scoot. Unfold, secure bolt (5 second install), scoot. While folded it’s easy to move it around on one wheel though.

Over happy with it and a lot of people ask about it since it’s so easy to use. The weight of the scooter is not bad, it’s a metal scooter with a big battery, it’s got some weight.

Will update if i have issues in the future but so far it’s working well for me

query: I'm looking for an easy and cost-effective way to regrip my golf clubs. I've had my clubs for around 10 years, and the grips are in bad shape. Can you guide me on how to use a grip kit effectively, including what additional supplies I might need, like solvent, and any tips for the regripping process? I want to ensure I do it right and have a good experience when playing with the new grips.
ori_review:
I'm not one of those golfers that buy a new set of clubs every year or so, and, after 10 years, the grips on my clubs were in bad shape. I purchased the Golf Pride kit and was able to completely re-grip my set of clubs in a couple of hours. The kit contains 13 grips (you need a different kind of grip for your putter), grip tape and a rubber vice grip (so you won't scratch your club when placing it in a vice). It does not include the grip solvent, which I purchased at a local golf shop earlier when I re-gripped my putter. The instructions tell you about other solvents you can use that can be purchased in a hardware store.

The process is easy:
- Remove the old grip and tape (I used a utility knife but be careful not to scratch the shaft) - be sure all the old tape is removed;
- Place the rubber vice grip on the shaft and place the club in the vice;
- Remove the plastic label from the new grip;
- Apply the tape to the end of the shaft, leaving about 1/4 inch or so overlap on the end (it makes it easier to start the grip on the shaft). The tape is double-sided, so you peel off one side, apply it to the shaft, and then peel off the other side;
- Apply the solvent to the tape - I just applied it to the top and used a finger to spread it out. This makes the tape slippery, activating the glue. Use plenty of solvent so the tape is very slippery.
- Place some solvent inside the grip itself and be sure the inside is coated;
- Finally, with the grip's label where you want it, slide the grip on the tape until it's completely on the club. You have a few seconds to position the logo as you want it.
- Set the club on the floor grip down to drain any solvent that might be remaining.

That's all there is to it. I played a round the next day with new grips and it felt great.

query: I'm looking for a solid and affordable barbell for my workouts. I need something that's about 5 feet long and can fit standard 1-inch plates. ori_review:
This bar is exactly what it says. 5' long, 1" wide (fits standard plates, NOT 2" OLYMPIC PLATE). Weighed about 12lbs on my scale. Really, I can't imagine getting a better value on this. Went to a few local stores, Walmart, Academy, etc, and couldn't find a place that beat the price. And this is a solid piece of metal, so no one could beat the quality either.

There are a few small things. There were small rough spots on the bar, like other people mentioned, but nothing that felt like it could be a problem during a workout. It looks like it could really comfortable fit 4-6 plates, but given that it claims a max of 250, you probably won't need more than 3.

The spinlock collars do slip a bit, and you'l have to re-tighten them as you exercise. I like doing bicep curls with it, so the swaying motion causes the plates to spin and the collars to start loosening. To address that, I added a small rubber washer before I put the plates on to help keep them more secure, and to add some tension to prevent loosening. I'll be adding photos of that later. This isn't 100% necessary, but the collars spin on so easily that it makes sense they loosen easily too.

FOR EXERCISES:
Seems a little short for bench pressing, so if you're looking to get into serious chest exercises (200lbs+), you might want to look for an 6' Olympic bar instead. But for lighter presses (~150lbs) it should be perfect. It's my favorite to use for bicep curls. Overhead presses for the shoulders are great here too. The only thing I don't 100% recommend: I like doing hip thrusts when I'm working my glutes, but at 1" thin, it does dig into you a bit if you've got it loaded with weights. Otherwise, really versatile given its size.

query: I'm looking for a jump rope that is lightweight and designed for speed, ideally one that allows for quick spinning and is suitable for advanced techniques like double-unders. I’ve heard some ropes can be hard to feel when swinging, which affects timing and rhythm. Is there a way to adjust the rope length easily, and how does the customer service of the company handle feedback on their products? Additionally, is it true that this type of rope isn’t recommended for beginners and requires some practice to get used to?
ori_review:
First off, this jump rope is great and terraFIT has the best customer service evar! They actually take customer feedback into account when designing/re-designing products!

Anyway, everything about this thing is small/svelte. The handles are small in diamter and very light, and the rope is a thin cable that is coated in plastic. The handles are an outer black plastic piece, with an inner white plastic piece that rotates and is connected to the rope. There is an adjustment in the handle to change how much movement/"play" there is between the two parts of the handle, and you want to double check that it is set loose enough for the inner white plastic piece to rotate freely.

The rope simply slides through eyelets at the ends of the handles and has two small metal stops that let you adjust the length of the rope, which you WILL need to do (it comes pretty long). They advise that once you have the rope length adjusted that you cut it to suit, so you don't have a bunch of extra rope swinging around.

The carrying case is a really nice touch.

All in all this is a fantastic jump rope that can achieve some crazy speeds because of how thing / light it is, VERY easy to spin it quick enough for double-unders. On the other hand the rope is so light that you pretty much cannot feel it swinging around you. IT IS VERY DIFFERENT THAN A ROPE BASED JUMP ROPE that you may have used in elementary school. A normal thick rope is easy to feel swinging around your body so you can pretty much feel when you should jump. WIth this TerraFit rope you MUST develop a rythym because you cannot tell where the rope is at very well. This is a skill that will take some time to develop if you aren't used to jumping rope a lot.
I read the reviews that said "not for beginners" and didn't understand what they meant, but it's the heft/weight of the rope that makes all the difference in the technique that you have to use. Once you get used to it though it's great!

End of the day this rope is worth buying for 3 reason 1) you can spin it super fast 2) it comes with a spare rope 3) terrafit is an awesome company.

query: I'm looking for a high-quality poncho liner that is made in the USA, but I'm concerned about the price. I want to know if the quality justifies the cost, especially compared to cheaper options that I've used before. How do the materials, stitching, and durability compare, and would it be worth it for field use despite being overpriced? Also, are there alternatives to buying new that still meet high standards?
ori_review:
This is a genuine, US made poncho liner, and the quality is top notch. However I do feel that it is way overpriced. It should cost no more than $50-$60. That said, I’ll note the differences between this genuine liner (henceforth referred to as “US” liner) and my USGI industries (made in China) liner (henceforth referred to as “China” liner) so that you can decide if it is worth purchasing for the insane price.
1. The stitching - the stitches on the US liner are closer together (I.e. there are more stitches per inch of fabric) and hence it is stronger and will stand more abuse than the China liner.

2.the trim around the liner perimeter - on the China liner, there is a gap where the trim overlaps itself, large enough to fit a finger or pen into it. This can potentially get snagged on something and result in a tear. On the US liner, wherever the trim overlaps itself the overlap is sewn shut, so there is no chance of it snagging. Also, on the US liner, the stitching that connects the trim to the main blanket is stitched higher up from the edge of the trim than on the China liner. This will prevent the fabric of the trim from coming loose easily. The trim stitching on the China liner is very close to the edge of the trim material.

3. The ropes/tie-outs - on US liner, the tie-outs are made of genuine, gutted milspec paracord. The China liner is made of some kind of synthetic rope material that is obviously not as strong and robust as the paracord and looks like it would easily fray/wear out from heavy use. The bartack stitching used to attach the tie outs to the liner is also more robust and better done on the US liner.

4. The Filling - the US liner has noticeably more filling than the China liner

These are the main differences that I’ve noticed. I wanted a liner that I could trust in the field, so I bit the bullet and bought this, but at home I sleep with my China liner. I’ve had the China liner for less than a year and some of the stitching is already beginning to come out. And that is simply from using it as a blanket on my bed. For home use, the China liner is definitely worth it due to its much lower price tag. If you want a genuine US quality liner for harder use, then you have to decide for yourself if it us worth paying double what the liner is worth. Another option is to buy a used one in good condition. You can get them around $40-$50 if you are Lucky. I hope this review was helpful.
In summary, it is top quality, but extremely overpriced

query: I'm looking for a compact and fuel-efficient stove that's great for backpacking and camping. I've been transitioning bulkier car camping gear to more backpacking oriented and this was highly recommended at REI. This is my first backpacking type stove and I love it! It's compact, easy to use, easily cook with other cookware and fuel efficient.

All the accessories nest well and you don't have to buy Jetboil brand fuel. We bought a canister of Coleman fuel from Walmart which worked just fine, cheaper and we used it for 7+ camping trips. If you are actually backpacking, I'd recommend the Jetboil brand since they are smaller and can fit nested inside the cup. Water boils very quickly and has taken no longer than 3-4 minutes. Pot adapter is included which is great in case you want to use other cookware besides the cup. Bottom plastic cup and the actual cooking cup have measurement markings which has been useful. The plastic sipping lid has holes on it which can be used as a strainer. The rubber grips have prevented burns. The twisting control handle is great for very controlled fuel burn. Fuel can stabilizer also comes with this which is useful in case you are trying to cook on a picnic table or something else that is uneven.

Here's the bad:
I don't have a lot of complaints but I do have to say there are other stoves out there that are cheaper. I found $150 to be pricey but in the end it was worth it due to all of the useful features and included accessories. The cup is also tricky to remove from the stove right after cooking since the cup is hot. query: I'm looking for a kayak loading assistant that sticks well to my vehicle's roof and helps me load my sea kayak more easily, especially since I'm doing this solo. ori_review:
A paddling buddy's kids got her one for Christmas, as we both used it on our first paddle of the year. I am a 66 year old woman with a 17.5' sea kayak going on the roof of a Dodge Caravan. I've heaved kayaks up onto roofs for decades, but at 40 the experience is somewhat easier.

"The Rolly Thing" sticks incredibly well to a clean car surface; window or metal. Wipe the surface first, do one side at a time (you'll need two hands).

The point is to lift HALF the boat at one time. Set the stern on the ground, lift the bow, lay it on the Rolly Thing, get behind the boat and shove. Rolly Thing keeps the boat on track, keeps it from sliding sideways as you load, makes your shoving it onto the roof easier, and is an all around useful object especially if you find yourself doing this solo.

I suspect it could be an additional support rack ON your roof (I need a block under my front bulkhead) but as with anything on your roof going down the road at 55mph, you need to tie it down/lash it to the boat as well as use the suction.

I got one of these rather than risking questionable quality of similar roller-loaders, because I had used it and KNOW it works. Another review I read compared three, and this one came out on top.

I'll add that the softer (but dense) foam of this roller keeps the boat from slipping and sliding.

query: I'm looking for a reliable bicycle lock setup that allows me to secure both my front and back wheels effectively. Is this lock design really effective against theft, and is it worth the price compared to other highly rated locks? I want something that I can carry easily and use for both short and long-term parking.
ori_review:
The Sheldon Brown method for safely securing your bike is to use a U-lock on the back wheel, threaded through the rear triangle, and a cable to secure the front wheel. I take this a step further, since I know that a cable lock is like warm butter to a set of bolt cutters, with a 2nd U-lock. Having one black lock and one white lock makes it really easy to know which key goes to which lock. I don't know if I could manage with 2 black locks.

query: How effective is this inversion table for alleviating lower back pain, especially for those with lumbar or sciatica issues? Also, what tips do you have for inspecting the parts and assembling the table to avoid any problems? Are there any specific recommendations for using the ankle braces securely for safety?
ori_review:
1st, please notice that inversion tables are designed for lower and middle back traction, and are NOT at anyway at all intended for C-Spine relief (around the neck.) If you have lower lumbar or sciatica problems, this is the ticket.

Open the box and INSPECT EVERYTHING BEFORE starting assembly. Check the welds, lay out the pieces so you know what is what, and DO NOT, repeat, DO NOT just cut the screws and bolts out until you need them (an exacto knife makes easy work of this.) Some folks have complained about welds and mismatched pieces, but I can't say the same for me. In fact, it's probably the most well packaged gizmo I've purchased in a while with every single piece plastic wrapped and then with foam inlays. Form fit and finish are A++

Assembly - Takes about an hour - do yourself a favor in advance and have a 13mm socket wrench, and 13mm box wrench handy. Save your knuckles and frustration levels and skip the lousy wrench that comes with it. The Allen wrench is perfectly fine for the couple of bolts that use it, and the phillips head on the end is fine too. As I mentioned, open the fasteners AS NEEDED. Here's a trick - lock the table flat when you are trying to put the foot bar on. Or have a helper. Way easier than trying to hold it up and get the pins in at the same time. Other than that, it's just a handful of nuts and bolts.

Use - I use mine barefoot in flip flops all the time. It's got foam ankle braces that (should) soften over time, but you can leave them out in the sun to help them soften up too. When you get on this thing, MAKE SURE THE ANKLE BRACES ARE AS TIGHT AS YOU CAN GET THEM. Remember, that's what's holding your entire body weight. Socks and sneakers will probably work for most people, but you have to get used to it. And again - tight as you can get it for safety.

Using an inversion table is not simply strapping in and hanging upside down for an hour. If you've ever had spinal traction, you know start slow, and traction should only be for a minute or 2 at a time. Don't jump right on and go for broke hanging at 90 degrees or you are going to be really sore. 2 minutes up for every 1 minute down to be safe. I usually do this 3x a day.

Happy hanging!

query: I'm looking for a portable and versatile travel spinning setup that can complement my travel casting setup. I want something that is easy to set up and break down, with good line markers. I've seen that some setups can feel a bit front heavy, so I'm curious if there are ways to balance it out. ori_review:
I've been looking for a versatile travel spinning setup to compliment my travel casting setup and this has been on my radar for some time. I took the leap and bought it based on reviews and gave it a true test. I went to a couple of my honey holes and caught some decent sized bass. My initial thought is that this setup and breakdown is a breeze on this rod and the line markers do help line things up. The finish reminds me of my 13 Fishing Omen rod and I love it! It looks like quality!

Make sure to spool your line without line twist because the first eyelet isn't that standard huge guide we're used to and may possibly limit cast distance. It didn't bother me at all and it seems to cast fine for weightless presentations. I was able to cast with control with a bit of practice. Balance wise it is a bit front heavy but it's expected from a telescoping setup. I've seen videos of people putting weights on the back (you can unscrew the butt of the pole and place weights in there) to counterbalance this so I'll give that a try.

While fishing I was able to feel everything from rocks, ledges, grass and stumps. I even felt blue gil nipping at my senko! It's almost comparable to my high end rigs! When I got a fish on (you can feel the bite it's wonderful) I was able to muscle the bass out of vegetation and then I tested the back bone out for boat flipping and durability. It passed those tests with flying colors.

In the end, I highly recommend this rod and will be using it when going on trips where I can't bring my main setups or when I go scout ponds for bass. If anything changes though I'll be sure to update here! I've got 6 months of warranty so I plan to use as much as I can but I'm not worried about this blank failing at all. Can't wait to see how it handles a 4#er!!!

My physical therapist introduced me to the mobo to treat tendinitis on the outside of my foot. Back story: about a year ago I was diagnosed with metatarsal neuritis, and the podiatrist put a metatarsal pad in my shoe. A couple of months ago the side of my foot started _really_ hurting, especially when getting out of bed in the morning. A (different) podiatrist said that was tendinitis and sent me to PT. Using the board forces you to really mobilize the ball of your foot. I definitely notice that I am walking much more pronated on that foot than I was before the mobo board. And the tendinitis rarely, if ever, bothers me anymore. I've probably used the board a total of 10 times by now, so I got results extremely quickly.

Eventually I am planning to try getting rid of the metatarsal pad, and see if my new, improved gait keeps my foot happy without it.

Update (3/2022): I've been getting along without the metatarsal pad for a month or two now and so far, so good!

And then for just running short errands or joy rides, I leave the chain at home & use my KKs only. This is a perfect system for me. query: I'm looking for a lightweight sleeping bag that can keep me warm in temperatures down to the 20s. I recently camped with my son, who is quite tall, and I need something that fits well for both of us. I prefer a bag that is easy to pack and doesn’t take up much space. I also want to ensure that it has a good cinch to keep the cold air out, as I experienced some cold on my feet during the trip. Ideally, I’d like a bag that is comfortable for both shorter and taller individuals, and I'd appreciate tips on what to wear inside it to stay warm, especially regarding layers. Would this sleeping bag be a good fit for those needs? Also, any recommendations for a lightweight tent would be helpful.
ori_review:
Camped this past weekend with my 14 year old son and some friends. I bought one of these for my son and one for me. Size wise- my son is 6'4, 180 lbs. I got him the "long" size bag. I am 5'7 and 130 lbs and bought a regular for myself. Both were excellent fits. Neither of us felt constrained. I had plenty of room. He said he did too.
Packing wise- these things are super easy to pack up. No major effort in stuffing them into the stuff bags. They cinch down great, don't take up much room and are super lightweight.
Warmth wise- air temps dipped down into the 20s. We were both wearing multiple layers, albeit me more than my son. (He's 14 and won't always listen, you all understand.) I even slept in my coat. With that said, I was perfectly warm, with the sole exception of my feet, but that's my own fault because I was only wearing one pair of wool socks and my feet are habitually cold anyway. My son said he got a LITTLE cold, but I don't think he wore enough layers. Even more impressive to me is that we were trying to do this trip pretty minimally. My boyfriend is former SF and strung us all up some sort of tarp contraptions about a foot or so off the ground, so none of us were even in a tent. It was pretty much this bag and nothing else between us and the air on the sides of us. Both my son and I had mats under us. His was thermal, mine was not. We both agreed that we felt warm under us. The top of the bags cinch up super tight and my son said he even got a little claustrophobic and was afraid he wouldn't be able to get out. Me, on the other hand, I found that cord and kept it pulled tight because that air was icy. There was snow under us and quite a bit of dew accumulated on us when the sun came up. Still warm and dry. Only thing I'm doing differently next time is bringing extra socks and investing in a lightweight Hyke and Byke tent because, neat as the poncho hooch was, I'm pretty certain I'd like a tent better.

query: I'm looking for a sleeping pad that is comfortable, lightweight, and packs down small enough to fit into a weekend bag. I’ve used many pads over the years and need one that provides a luxurious sleeping experience without taking up too much space in my pack. I also want something that is easy to inflate and has features like an integrated pump and pillow. Can the Nemo Cosmo meet these needs, and how does it compare to other high-end options in terms of comfort and insulation?
ori_review:
I believe this is the best sleeping pad I've ever seen. Five Stars.
I used to be a rock climbing guide. I guess I was super hard core. LOL. I spent quite a lot of time hiking and camping and sleeping out doors. Because of this I have had the pleasure of owning most of the sleeping pads that have been available since the 1990's. Most of the good ones were the wonderful Therm-A-Rest self-inflating products: thick and thin, short and long, shaped and rectangular. And there are the cheep ones, the cool z-fold ones, and the several varieties of dense closed-cell foam (military grade and nicer REI blue gel-type ones).
Having said that, most all of them are variations of the same theme: they're big, they take a up a lot of valuable real estate, and if you want to have enough insulation that you can tell they're there, they need to be pretty thick. They either just barely fit in a pack (taking up too much valuable real estate), or you have to strap them to the outside of your pack, also taking up valuable real estate - especially if you are carrying both camping and climbing gear....

When I was shopping for this I was primarily looking for a pad that would be comfortable, light and not take up much space. I wanted one that would easily fit INTO a weekend bag for packing light, maybe traveling without a tent. I was envisioning doing some self-contained bicycle packing, and longer multi-day solo trips.

That's what I like about this Nemo Cosmo. It's really neat, it's a little different, and compared to any other pad I'd want to sleep on, it packs down really really small. With no real effort mine packs down to a 5.5" x 10" cylinder. It weighs about the same as the other medium-thick pads, but once it is inflated it is actually VERY thick. Mucho Grande thick. Now, I realize this is not THE LIGHTEST nor the SMALLEST pad out there. But I believe it is one of the THICKEST and most LUXURIOUSLY COMFORTABLE ones. Sometimes life is full of wonderful little compromises, but at 2lbs 4 oz, there's not much compromise here. The Nemo Cosmo comes with its own carry sack and an integrated repair kit. However, after how small it gets, the feature that most sets it apart from its competition it is its integrated 'soft' foot pump. If you get a chance to actually play with a bunch of the different pads out there, this is a really BIG deal. Most of them are a real pain to inflate, they take forever, or they require some special additional apparatus that costs more money..... The Nemo Cosmo has a non-intrusive, integrated pump, and it Freaking Rocks! It takes me about 30-45 seconds of casual foot pumping effort to fully inflate the pad. Using just the pump it is easy to over inflate the pad until it feels too hard -- which is perfect because next to the integrated pillow there is a handy little screw-valve so that once you lay down you can easily let air out and 'fine tune' the pressure to whatever feels right. Yep, there's an integrated pillow too. Not only that, but all the pump mechanism and intake/exhaust valves are down at your feet, so they won't ever bother you while sleeping. They say this Insulated version of the Nemo Cosmo 'has a layer of PrimaLoft." This appears to be a thin layer of fleece laminated to the inside of the top half of the pad. It feels like its about the thickness of your standard fleece sweater, which is not a lot of insulation compared to the expanding foam Therm-A-Rest pads. Then again, without a pad, I almost never feel cold from the ground. I am am much more likely to feel the hardness or the bumpiness: I would prefer to have a more comfortable sleeping pad over a more insulated one. If I was sleeping on snow or somewhere properly frozen I don't know if this Nemo Cosmo would be the best pad for me, but it might me. And the last detail is a minor one, but I like how the baffles of the air chamber run side to side, not lengthwise along the pad. Why? I don't want the pad to 'wrap up' around me as I sink into the middle. The horizontal baffles seem to offer more consistent support than lengthwise ones.

I am a recovering Gear nerd. Before I spent $150 buying yet another sleeping pad, I spent a good bit of time reading up on ALL the pads currently available, then I went to several major retailers of the high-end good ones (places like REI) and spent several hours at each physically fiddled with, inflating and laying on all the interesting ones. I had conversations with the people who sold the various pads. I LOVE smart attention to details. I care a LOT about little things like fit and finish, simplicity in design, about seam strength, and whether or not a product FEELS solid and durable. I care a lot about comfort and aesthetics.
I am kind of shocked to say it, but the Nemo Cosmo exceeds all my expectations, I think it is noticeably better than the other pads out there, and I expect it bless many adventures with a good night's sleep.

query: I'm looking for a workout bench that is easy to assemble and feels solid without wobbling. Can you provide tips on how to avoid issues during assembly, like handling the bolts and washers? Also, what should I do if I can't find the allen wrench needed for assembly? Finally, how can I ensure that I don't accidentally stack washers when putting it together? For my workouts with dumbbells, I need something reliable and durable that fits my budget.
ori_review:
The bench assembled easily and feels solid with no wobbling. My first work out with the new bench went well. I'll only work out with dumbbells, so I don't envision any issues in terms of weight loads.

A few recommendations...

1. Be careful when opening the shipping box. The package that contains the bolts and washers had opened in transit. Had I opened the box in the wrong area, it could have been a bear to find the washers after they spilled out. Fortunately, I opened the shipping box on the living room carpet, so it was easy to corral the runaway washers.

2. Do not tighten any of the bolts until you have all of the bolts in and they've begun to thread. You have to jiggle things a bit to get all holes lined up. If you tighten things down ahead of time, you won't be able to jiggle the pieces enough to get all of the bolts threaded.

3. There is an allen wrench provided in the shipment. (It was the only tool I needed to complete the assembly.) At first, I didn't see it and thought I'd have to head to the store to buy a metric allen wrench to tighten the bolts, but as I rummaged through the packaging material, the allen wrench appeared. I'm not sure if it was in the same package as the bolts and washers and had broken free, or if it was free swimming in the box. Anyway, it is there, so keep an eye out for it.

4. The washers tend to cling to one another, so it is easy to put two washers on a bolt and not notice. I ended up thinking I was two washers short as I was ready to put the last two bolts into place. On closer examination, I noticed two of the partially inserted bolts had two washers on them.

For the price and for my purpose, it fits the bill.

I waited a long time to write a review. I think the seller sent me a bunch of emails wanting me to at first.

Sometimes the zippers get a little stuck on the covers but thats ok.

The backpack is extremely light. If you had nothing in it you would forget you had it on its so light.

The ONLY Con to this and I want to tell the manufacturer or seller of this about it through the Q & As. There should be a double layer on the back side of backpack on the inside for sweat. My sweat goes right through the backpack and gets whatever's in there wet. If they had a water resistant double layer on the back side this would be the best hiking backpack in the world. I actually wouldn't mind if it had somehow had 4 bottle holders but I guess thats not possible unless they had some on the front. Otherwise I got 2 extra bottles in the bag itself which you sort of feel hitting your back. Though if you are bike riding of course you can just put 2 on your bike

Overall, a great buy!

query: I'm looking for a rope saw that can help me cut high limbs from hardwood trees effectively. ori_review: Product worked to cut a 4” limb and a 2” limb of a hardwood tree. Limbs were 20 and 25 ft off the ground. For that alone, 5 stars.  Some reviewers say it cut like butter.  Nonsense. It takes time and effort to figure out the best technique to cut.  The blade has a tendency to catch and so you need to work the blade in different directions and tensions to free it to resume cutting. When the blade is free you can make long strokes. When it binds, all you can do are short strokes. As with any saw, smooth light sawing gets the job done faster than brute force.  Finally, some reviewers mention uneven cuts of big branches. I had same issue.  Solution is to first cut the branch a foot or two from trunk.  Come back and cut the stub.  Definitely more work, but a professional result.

query: I'm looking for a lightweight helmet that provides good ventilation and comes in multiple sizes for a comfortable fit. I want to ensure it offers protection in case of a fall, but I'm also curious about its design and any potential comfort adjustments. Can you recommend a helmet that meets these needs?
ori_review:
This helmet provides protection on many levels. Not only might it save your life should you take a spill (which happens to everyone eventually), but it will also likely reduce the rate of pregnancy by making you seem a bit...mushroom shaped . This second feature is not unique to this particular helmet, but it might be nice if manufactures would thrust their design teams at the secondary issue beyond impact protection.

Some key features:
* This skull cap comes in several sizes, so you don't have to worry about it being too tight or too loose. The small might even be a good cap for little johnny.

* Veins running through the top allow for good ventilation. Things get a little hotter than if I'm free-riding, but the consequences of an unplanned spill make this brain barrier well worth the trouble.

* Easy to strap on, though the bits that dangle over my lobes hang at a funny angle. I'm not sure why they make the place where the webbing forks naturally sit at 90 degrees to the chinstrap.

* There's a little knub you can reach around to for making fine fit adjustments. It's a little hard discover at first, but once you know where it is you'll want to fiddle around with it for maximum comfort.

* Very light weight. I'm not saying it will feel like it isn't there, but it doesn't get in the way too much either.

I don't want to give Giro the shaft on this review just for the look of the thing, it functions just as its creator intended

query: I'm looking for a flint striker that creates a lot of sparks. I've tried a couple of different scrapers, but I've heard that the Super Scraper from Firesteel.com performs better. Can you help me find a striker that is similar in thickness and sharpness to the Super Scraper, but perhaps even lighter and easy to use, or suggest if I should stick with the Super Scraper for optimal performance? I also want to know if ditching the scrapers that come with my current flint is a good idea.
ori_review:
A flint is a flint, it's the striker that makes all the difference.

I have the flint from Firesteel.com and from Coghlan. The only difference between the sparks I create from the two is due
to the striker. The 'Super Scraper' from Firesteel.com makes more sparks and it easier to strike. The Super Scraper is thicker
and has a sharper edge and this makes a whole lot of difference. When I strike my Coghlan flint with the Super Scraper I get the same amount of sparks as I do when I strike it on the Firesteel.com flint. Therefore, it's not the flint but the striker that make the difference.

The opposite side of the sharpen edge of the blade of my Spyderco pocket knife has as similar thick right angle as the Super Scraper and it gives me a similar spark as the Super Scraper. However, the Super Scraper is lighter and attaches to my flint with a lanyard.

Ditch the scrapers that come from the Colghan, Light My Fire, etc. and either get the Super Scraper or use something similar the Super Scraper. BTW the Super Scraper is @2.5mm thick and the edge is a right angle and where the angles meet, it kinda feels 'sharp' but not the kind of sharp that you get from a knife... I hope you understand what I am trying to mean.

query: I'm interested in getting a trike, but I've read that there can be some initial challenges with assembly and setup. Can you provide tips on what to expect during the assembly process? Also, I’ve noticed some reviews mention the color and packaging issues. Is the bike really more of a silvery blue than a darker slate? Lastly, can you suggest any modifications for comfort, especially regarding the seat, since I'm looking for something suitable for longer rides?
ori_review:
I bought this bike after reading every single review, both positive and negative. I even took the step of ordering the bike from Amazon's Warehouse Deals. I paid a very reasonable price. I am a 52 year old woman who does not really have a lot of mechanical experience, but it was a beautiful day when the bike arrived. I got my iced tea and sat on my porch with the box and spent a leisurely afternoon figuring it out. With only a little help from my husband and son (mostly to just confirm I did something correctly) I was able to assemble the bike. I'm glad I did, too, because now, adjustments make more sense to me...I know the parts and understand how they work and fit together.

That said, if you are just hoping for a quick experience putting it together, you may want to get help or pay a bike shop. I rate the bike 5 stars because I love the style and I think it was a GREAT value. It seems to be working well. But for the sake of those who read reviews, here are some notes that might help you.

--The color: I read a lot of reviews that complained that they were hoping for a more BLUE bike. This should be called "Ice Blue" or something like that, not Slate, because the bike is really a silvery blue not a darker color like I would think Slate would be.

--Packaging: I ordered from Amazon Warehouse Deals, which said the item would be repackaged, so I expected that. The large box it came in was not TOO badly roughed up from shipping, but when I opened it, the inner box that was holding all the bike parts was fairly frightening. Torn spots, dents in the cardboard, etc. From reading a lot of reviews about dents, I wonder if shipping is just really hard on this. Mine came basically double boxed. I wonder if someone returned it because of the condition of the original box! The original box did not appear to ever have been opened and resealed? Anyway, I probably got lucky, but my guess is this is a shipping issue and perhaps unavoidable when you have parts, like fenders, that are easily bent out of shape.

--Assembly: Yeah, there were a few head scratching moments where I had to look at the diagram, re-read and THINK, but I figured them out. I saw a YouTube video of a guy who was pretty mechanical and putting this bike together for one of his parents and he had pretty much the same issues I had! I used (after googling!) Vicks VapoRub for grease for the handlebar stem and it is working great. Did have to laugh at the whiff of menthol I got just before my second ride on it, when I adjusted the handlebars. Vaseline would work too if you don't have a tube of grease that they call for. I confirmed with a mechanical friend that this will be no problem, we're not dealing with high temperatures or huge amounts of friction. I had to really work to get fenders lined up to the holes for the bolts that hold them on, then I had to bend them into shape a little to keep them from rubbing. This is no big deal to me, but if it is to you, you're forewarned. If you can't find the stem for the seat, look inside the hole in the frame, lots of people think they don't have one then find it there! Brakes might take a while to get them adjusted properly. If any of this really doesn't sound like something you want to mess with then definitely find a handier friend or take it to a bike shop for assembly. I didn't mind the tweaking.

--Riding: THIS IS DIFFERENT THAN A TWO WHEEL BIKE! You have to really remember this or you may think something is wrong when it is not. If you learned to ride a two wheel bike, you instinctively *lean* to keep balance. Leaning on this bike is not necessary and may even make your sensation of being off balance WORSE. You *might* even want to lean OUT of a turn (the opposite direction) a tiny bit! I did feel a bit wonky on this trike at first, but I just took a deep breath and tried to remember that this was different. Much better as time goes on! Also, the road where I live is slightly graded to allow rain to runoff so if I'm riding on the road, I realize that it is going to feel off balance. I only take the road for a short while, then I am on the rails-to-trails near our home. That too is ever-so-slightly graded for runoff, but I can work with it better there. If the trail is clear, I just take my spot up the middle and my fellow bikers let me know they are coming with a friendly call or ring of their bell and I move over. :)

--Mount/Dismount: At first, I kept whacking the back of my legs with the back wheels. Just needed to get in the habit of remembering that unlike a 2 wheel bike, I have to watch for them.

--Seat: I'm a middle aged woman with an ample middle aged figure. The seat is just *okay* for me but since I got such a nice price on the bike, I don't feel badly about seeking out a wider, more comfortable seat. Until switching the seat, I only had gone about 3 miles at a time to avoid a sore posterior.

If you want a flawless, seamless experience to get up and running, look elsewhere or get professional help to assemble and fine tune. If you're willing to deal with a few little issues, you'll have a great trike at a great price.

query: Why should I consider using trekking poles for hiking, especially if I'm not looking to spend a lot? I’ve been hesitant about them but have heard they could really help with my hiking stamina and knee pain. What features should I look for in affordable poles, and how can I ensure I'm using them correctly to avoid issues?
ori_review:
My husband and I have been avid hikers over the past 15 years. But we poo-pood trekking poles. I would see other hikers slide using them and thought they would just get in the way.
This spring we were getting ready to complete the ADK Firetower Challenge. We needed to hike 5 mountains in 6 days. I joined a Facebook group about these hikes. And that is where I realized trekking poles would be beneficial. We didn’t want to spend a lot of money on poles that would only get used 5-10 times a year. Someone in the group recommended these. As soon as I read Ken and Cathy’s review (after laughing so hard), I knew if they liked the poles, so would we.
Well, they are the best! And I will never hike without them again. We have used them on trails that were dry, wet, snow covered, and even ice. Through mud and creeks. I feel they help my cardio stamina going up trails. And oh man, the difference in my knees going down! Worth every penny. Now I did watch a ton of you tube videos on how to measure for best height. And where to position them when going up or down mountains. . Just like when I was learning the best way to kayak, I found just do what works for you. When I had the poles at the height recommended going down mountains, my knees still hurt. When I raised them higher, that was my magic spot! So experiment with height and placement. These poles have kept me from sliding on my tush quite a few times. And at 66, I’m doing all I can to avoid falling.
I love these poles so much, when I saw them at an even cheaper price than I paid for them earlier this year, I bought another pair. Same color.
READ THE DIRECTIONS! I am quite confident that any of the negative reviews were due to user error.
Open the latch before tightening them. Check the latch before each use. I have had to tighten them on occasion. I put my full weight on each pole to test before use, and have never had the pole collapse on me. They fold up nicely to a manageable size when not in use. I love that it comes with extra tip, and accessories for mud, and snow.
There is no need to spend a fortune on trekking poles. We ran into a retired mountain hiking tour guide on one of our hikes. He and his friend both were using these poles. He said in all of his years as a tour guide, he tried several poles, and found the Trail Buddy to be the best.
Do not hesitate to buy these. You won’t regret it.

It should come with good accessories, like a leash and a carrying strap, and I need it to be durable enough for frequent use. Can you recommend a board that matches these needs and has a good reputation for quality?
ori_review:
For reference, I bought this for frequent ocean use. I live on a tropical island and already own to solid boards: one Naish and one Vesl. Both of those boards, the Vesl in particular, are high quality. The boards are primarily used within a lagoon where water is fairly calm, though we also use our SUPs for easy surfing when swells are there. My 12-yr old loves the Vesl but that's also my favorite so I went searching for inflatables as something he can use. After reading a lot of reviews and looking for something with the same dimensions as my Vesl (shorter and wider than the Naish for more stability), I settled on the Roc. I bought it from Amazon Warehouse so it was a bit of a gamble.

Out of the box, it looked unused and all components were present. I used the included pump and timed myself. 5 1/2 minutes continuous, though easy pumping without trying to "race". Definitely broke a sweat but it wasn't difficult to pump up at all. Please note (and this may be obvious already): the gauge will not register psi until the board appears mostly inflated. From there (5 psi), the pumping gets a little more difficult but goes quick. I stopped at 12 psi since I knew this would always be used in the hot sun. After pumping it, I stored it for 4 days to check for any leaks. Still registers at 12 psi after that.

I left this inflated and strapped it to the top of my car, along with one of my solid boards. 15' straps were perfect for this set up. If you were strapping two inflatable SUPs to the top, you'd need 20' straps since the inflatables are thicker than the solids. This is also pretty small once collapsed and stored in the included bag, so it wouldn't be difficult to set it up at the beach.

First impressions in somewhat choppy water with a strong current (both from a distant tropical storm): this board is stable and cuts through the water fairly quick. Had no trouble staying together between this board and the Vesl. It definitely feels a little different...not squishy per se, but just not the same as a solid board. The foam grip pad is great, the handle works well and isn't bothersome, the straps and D-rings are fantastic inclusions for this board. The paddle feels heavy compared to my carbon fiber paddle, but the cool thing is that it adjusts to a lower height than my other one, so my 12-yr old can use this with a proper fit. I also like that it initially floats. It doesn't stay floating, but it doesn't need to--you have enough time to pluck it from the water if you fall off.

I appreciated that this came with everything right out of the box. The leash is of good quality and looks nearly identical to my coiled Dakine leash. There was an included carrying strap for the board, once inflated, in case someone needs to carry it far down a beach or anything. The backpack/duffel is impressively well constructed. The fin is easy to attach and detach, and you get a high quality small dry bag (looks just like my expensive ScubaPro one) for phone, keys, etc. All in all...I am super impressed. Time will tell how it holds up, but I'm surprised what it comes with at this price point. Great board to learn on, nice and stable, would be great for SUP yoga as well.

ori_review: Assembly was very easy.  I use it while sitting on my sofa.  Two things to know:  (1)You need to brace the stand's base  against something at least on one side to keep it from "creeping" and (2)while the straps on the pedals do a great job, you need to sit high enough to keep your heel from hitting the ground. But it will be a real workout at higher tension levels.  Well made product!
